catalog_quote: Enrico 1991:111-121 (as carried by StressTyp2): "In level tone words, the pattern is simple. The final syllable gets main stress and all alternates before it get secondary stress. When there are both high and low tones in a word, the pattern is more complicated. The last high tone gets main stress. All alternates before it and the last syllable and alternates before it get secondary stress." | de Lacy 2002:23, (32): "(32) lists a number of languages in which tone is the primary factor in determining the position of stress ... b. Stress the rightmost high-toned syllable, else the rightmost syllable Golin Bunn & Bunn (1970), Bunn (1974) Masset Haida Enrico (1991 : 111ff)"

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'weight' (unbounded, tone-driven: main stress on the rightmost high-toned syllable, else the final syllable) is correct for Masset Haida and is supported three ways in copies we hold: (i) the StressTyp2-carried Enrico 1991:111-121 passage (verbatim in the held StressTyp2 dump), (ii) de Lacy 2002:23 ex.(32b) and de Lacy 2007 ex.(26), both confirmed verbatim in held author-copy PDFs, and (iii) -- not yet used by the record -- Enrico's own open sketch, Enrico 1989 'The Haida Language' p.225 item 6, 'Word stress in Masset has the last high-tone syllable in the word (if there is one) main-stressed, otherwise the word-final syllable is main-stressed'. Recommended upgrade: move the grade from 'quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2' to an opened primary quote by citing Enrico 1989:225 (open ANLA PDF, author's own words) alongside the StressTyp2 ca

sources.note: The deciding source itself (pp.111-121 on word stress and foot structure); our quote is the StressTyp2 carry, never opened. Would settle the secondary-stress rule and whether syllable weight (heavy nuclei) as well as high tone constrains footing, as Enrico 1986c fn.2 suggests.
